Exercises

Problems to check your understanding of this chapter. The solutions are folded away — try them yourself first.

Easy

1Easy

Three Cobb-Douglas consumers have parameters a=(0.4,0.5,0.6)a = (0.4, 0.5, 0.6)a=(0.4,0.5,0.6), wealths wi=50w_i = 50wi​=50, and p2=1p_2 = 1p2​=1. At p1=2p_1 = 2p1​=2, find each consumer's x1ix_1^ix1i​ and aggregate demand X1X_1X1​.

x1i(p1)=aiwip1x_1^i(p_1) = \frac{a_i w_i}{p_1}x1i​(p1​)=p1​ai​wi​​
  • Aggregating Demand
Show solution
  1. x11=0.4⋅50/2=10x_1^1 = 0.4 \cdot 50 / 2 = 10x11​=0.4⋅50/2=10, x12=0.5⋅50/2=12.5x_1^2 = 0.5 \cdot 50 / 2 = 12.5x12​=0.5⋅50/2=12.5, x13=0.6⋅50/2=15x_1^3 = 0.6 \cdot 50 / 2 = 15x13​=0.6⋅50/2=15.
  2. Adding up, X1=10+12.5+15=37.5X_1 = 10 + 12.5 + 15 = 37.5X1​=10+12.5+15=37.5. Aggregate demand is just the sum of individual demands — the definition of a "market demand curve" itself.

Medium

2Medium

Suppose each consumer iii satisfies Walras' law p⋅xi(p,wi)=wip \cdot x^i(p, w_i) = w_ip⋅xi(p,wi​)=wi​ (no assumption on the functional form of demand). Prove that aggregate demand X(p)=∑ixi(p,wi)X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i)X(p)=∑i​xi(p,wi​) satisfies p⋅X(p)=∑iwip \cdot X(p) = \sum_i w_ip⋅X(p)=∑i​wi​.

X(p)=∑ixi(p,wi)X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i)X(p)=i∑​xi(p,wi​)
  • Aggregating Demand
Show solution
  1. The inner product is linear in addition, so p⋅X(p)=p⋅∑ixi(p,wi)=∑ip⋅xi(p,wi)p \cdot X(p) = p \cdot \sum_i x^i(p, w_i) = \sum_i p \cdot x^i(p, w_i)p⋅X(p)=p⋅∑i​xi(p,wi​)=∑i​p⋅xi(p,wi​).
  2. Applying individual Walras' law to each term gives ∑ip⋅xi(p,wi)=∑iwi\sum_i p \cdot x^i(p, w_i) = \sum_i w_i∑i​p⋅xi(p,wi​)=∑i​wi​. The shape of demand (Cobb-Douglas or not) was never used — because summation is a linear operation.
    p⋅X(p)=∑ip⋅xi(p,wi)=∑iwip \cdot X(p) = \sum_i p \cdot x^i(p, w_i) = \sum_i w_ip⋅X(p)=i∑​p⋅xi(p,wi​)=i∑​wi​
3Medium

Two identical-taste Cobb-Douglas consumers with a=1/2a = 1/2a=1/2, total wealth W=100W = 100W=100, p1=1p_1 = 1p1​=1, p2=1p_2 = 1p2​=1. Compute X1X_1X1​ for the splits s=0.25s = 0.25s=0.25 and s=0.75s = 0.75s=0.75, and verify that individual demands change while aggregate demand does not.

  • The Representative Consumer
Show solution
  1. With s=0.25s = 0.25s=0.25, w1=25w_1 = 25w1​=25 and w2=75w_2 = 75w2​=75, so x11=12.5x_1^1 = 12.5x11​=12.5, x12=37.5x_1^2 = 37.5x12​=37.5, and the sum is X1=50X_1 = 50X1​=50.
  2. With s=0.75s = 0.75s=0.75, w1=75w_1 = 75w1​=75 and w2=25w_2 = 25w2​=25, so x11=37.5x_1^1 = 37.5x11​=37.5, x12=12.5x_1^2 = 12.5x12​=12.5 — the individual demands swap, but X1=50X_1 = 50X1​=50 is unchanged. Both equal X1=aW/p1=0.5⋅100=50X_1 = aW/p_1 = 0.5 \cdot 100 = 50X1​=aW/p1​=0.5⋅100=50.

Hard

4Hard

Suppose III consumers have indirect utilities of the Gorman form vi(p,wi)=αi(p)+b(p) wiv_i(p, w_i) = \alpha_i(p) + b(p)\,w_ivi​(p,wi​)=αi​(p)+b(p)wi​ with a common b(p)>0b(p) > 0b(p)>0. Use Roy's identity to derive each demand, prove that aggregate demand X(p)X(p)X(p) depends only on total wealth W=∑iwiW = \sum_i w_iW=∑i​wi​, and exhibit a representative consumer's indirect utility reproducing it.

vi(p,wi)=αi(p)+b(p) wiv_i(p, w_i) = \alpha_i(p) + b(p)\,w_ivi​(p,wi​)=αi​(p)+b(p)wi​
  • The Representative Consumer
Show solution
  1. Roy's identity xi=−∇pvi/∂vi/∂wx^i = -\nabla_p v_i / \partial v_i / \partial wxi=−∇p​vi​/∂vi​/∂w gives numerator −(∇αi(p)+∇b(p) wi)-(\nabla \alpha_i(p) + \nabla b(p)\,w_i)−(∇αi​(p)+∇b(p)wi​) and denominator b(p)b(p)b(p), so xi(p,wi)=−∇αi(p)b(p)−∇b(p)b(p) wix^i(p, w_i) = -\frac{\nabla \alpha_i(p)}{b(p)} - \frac{\nabla b(p)}{b(p)}\,w_ixi(p,wi​)=−b(p)∇αi​(p)​−b(p)∇b(p)​wi​.
  2. Summing over iii, the common b(p)b(p)b(p) gives X(p)=−∑i∇αi(p)b(p)−∇b(p)b(p) WX(p) = -\frac{\sum_i \nabla \alpha_i(p)}{b(p)} - \frac{\nabla b(p)}{b(p)}\,WX(p)=−b(p)∑i​∇αi​(p)​−b(p)∇b(p)​W — individual wealths enter only through total wealth WWW. The distribution is irrelevant to aggregate demand.
    X(p)=−∑i∇αi(p)b(p)−∇b(p)b(p) WX(p) = -\frac{\sum_i \nabla \alpha_i(p)}{b(p)} - \frac{\nabla b(p)}{b(p)}\,WX(p)=−b(p)∑i​∇αi​(p)​−b(p)∇b(p)​W
  3. Representative consumer: a single consumer with indirect utility V(p,W)=∑iαi(p)+b(p) WV(p, W) = \sum_i \alpha_i(p) + b(p)\,WV(p,W)=∑i​αi​(p)+b(p)W reproduces exactly this X(p)X(p)X(p) via Roy's identity. The Gorman form (common marginal utility of wealth b(p)b(p)b(p)) is thus sufficient for a representative consumer to exist.
